newsitem.title: MEXICO: Telmex Q1 solid, but feels rivals pinch.
newsitem.headline: Telmex Q1 solid, but feels rivals pinch.

text.p: Mexican telephone company Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex) weathered its first ever quarter of competition but showed signs that its bottom line will eventually take a hit from new rivals, analysts said.
As expected by analysts, Telmex reported slightly weaker first quarter net profits as competition slowly got underway and the Mexican economy remained weak from its recent recession.
Telmex registered net profits of 3.207 billion pesos, off 26 percent compared to the same quarter in 1996.
Earnings per ADR was $0.96 -- very close to the $0.95 per ADR forecast by a Reuters survey of four industry analysts.

"There were no real surprises, although the results were much cleaner than in previous quarters, when they had a lot of one-time charges," said Leslie Marcus, an analyst at Santander Investment in New York.
Like most Mexican companies during the first quarter, Telmex's bottom line was artificially hurt by lower foreign exchange gains and monetary gains on its income statement.
On an operating basis, things looked better. Telmex's operating profits were 4.9 billion pesos during the quarter, up 5.6 percent on the 4.645 billion during the year-ago quarter.
But there are some signs Telmex's top line is beginning to feel the effects of competition, analysts said.
International long-distance revenues fell 20.8 percent during the quarter to 2.936 billion pesos, mostly from discounts in pricing by Telmex.
More ominously, international long-distance minutes grew by just 8.5 percent, compared to 20.5 percent and 14.4 percent in the third and fourth quarters of 1996, respectively.

On a per-minute basis, international long-distance revenues were 3.23 pesos, slightly lower than some expectations. That compares to international long-distance per-minute revenues of 4.05 pesos during the last quarter of 1996.
"It is obvious the effects of competition are starting to be felt, but they haven't yet filtered through to the bottom line," said Robert Hulme, an analyst at Interacciones brokerage in New York.

Line growth was also weak during the quarter, at 0.4 percent annual growth. The overall number of lines installed did grow slightly during the quarter, however, after two consecutive quarters of declines.
While revenues were a fraction weaker than some expected, it appears Telmex did a good job in controlling operating costs, analysts said.
"The top-line was very much in-line with our forecasts, although we were on the low end. But costs came in well below our expectations," said Pat Jurczak, an analyst at ING Barings in New York.
Analysts stressed it was too early to tell how well the former monopoly will hold up as competition spreads to the entire country during the second and third quarters.
Jurczak estimated Telmex had lost between four to five percent of the market so far.
Santander's Marcus said higher volumes from lower prices plus an economic recovery in Mexico could help offset market share loss in the coming quarters.
